newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss bankers meet Berne envoy on Holocaust funds.
newsitem.headline: Swiss bankers meet Berne envoy on Holocaust funds.

text.p: Switzerland's diplomatic troubleshooter will meet top bankers and executives on Monday to discuss ways of countering accusations the Swiss pocketed Holocaust bank accounts and accepted Nazi loot.

Diplomat Thomas Borer said on Thursday the meeting would be an exchange of views as part of his task of formulating a government strategy for defending Switzerland against a bruising wave of allegations it profited cynically from World War Two.
"It is a matter of reaching a common view of the situation so that I can propose the proper strategies to the cabinet," Borer told Reuters.
Borer said the talks would bring together the heads of the biggest banks and insurance companies as well as senior people from the Swiss National Bank and the Swiss Federation of Industry.

"It's a normal meeting with leaders of business, especially the big banks and big insurers," he said but declined to confirm that the banks would include the three biggest -- Union Bank of Switzerland, Swiss Bank Corp and Credit Suisse.

Banks and to a lesser extent insurers have been hit by allegations they are sitting on huge Jewish accounts left by Holocaust victims, although a bank ombudsman this week said only 11,000 Swiss francs ($8,666) had been found so far in five ownerless Jewish accounts.

"I have to know their problems and their view of the situation. I am doing the same with the Swiss ambassadors on Friday," he said, referring to an unusual conference of Swiss envoys to European countries, the U.S. and Israel called home for the meeting.
Borer is in charge of a diplomatic task force created to toughen Berne's often meek responses to a wave of criticism from world Jewish groups and influential U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato.
The task force was set up by Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti in late October as the government went on the offensive after weeks of leaving the issue to lower-ranking officials and Swiss bankers.
Borer will also meet a leading British critic of Switzerland on Monday, opposition Labour member of parliament and World Jewish Congress vice-president Greville Janner.
Janner will see Cotti, Borer's task force and Swiss parliamentarians on an invitation issued by Berne after Janner demanded the Swiss pay for Nazi gold bought during World War Two.

Janner has pressed Switzerland for renegotiation of a 1946 agreement between Berne and the Allied powers on dividing gold the Swiss National Bank bought from Hitler's Germany, some of which was stolen from countries and people under Nazi rule.
Berne has rejected the possibility of renegotiating a valid international treaty 50 years later.
